proof_nl:
For k=1 there is only one permutation of {1}, namely (1). The sign condition is vacuous, and the last entry 1 is the first smallest element. Hence v^(1)_1=1, so v^(1)=(1).

Now fix k with 1<=k<=n-1 and fix j with 1<=j<=k+1. Because a permutation of {1,...,k} has entries exactly 1,...,k, saying that its last entry is the i-th smallest is equivalent to saying that its last entry equals i. Likewise, for a permutation of {1,...,k+1}, saying that its last entry is the j-th smallest is equivalent to saying that its last entry equals j.

For 1<=i<=k, let C_i be the set of permutations c=(c_1,...,c_k) of {1,...,k} such that s_t(c_{t+1}-c_t)>0 for all 1<=t<k and c_k=i. Then |C_i|=v^(k)_i.

Let B_j be the set of permutations b=(b_1,...,b_{k+1}) of {1,...,k+1} such that s_t(b_{t+1}-b_t)>0 for all 1<=t<=k and b_{k+1}=j. Then |B_j|=v^(k+1)_j.

Define phi_j on {1,...,k} by phi_j(x)=x if x<j and phi_j(x)=x+1 if x>=j. This is a strictly increasing bijection from {1,...,k} onto {1,...,k+1} minus {j}. For c in C_i, define T_j(c)=(phi_j(c_1),...,phi_j(c_k),j). Then T_j(c) is a permutation of {1,...,k+1} whose last entry is j.

Because phi_j is strictly increasing, it preserves all order comparisons: for 1<=t<k, c_{t+1}>c_t if and only if phi_j(c_{t+1})>phi_j(c_t), and similarly c_{t+1}<c_t if and only if phi_j(c_{t+1})<phi_j(c_t). Therefore for 1<=t<k we have s_t(phi_j(c_{t+1})-phi_j(c_t))>0 exactly when s_t(c_{t+1}-c_t)>0. So the first k-1 sign conditions are preserved.

Now c_k=i. Hence the k-th entry of T_j(c) is phi_j(i), which equals i if i<j and equals i+1 if i>=j. Therefore j-phi_j(i)>0 exactly when i<j, and j-phi_j(i)<0 exactly when i>=j. It follows that:
if s_k=+1, then T_j(c) belongs to B_j exactly for those c with i<j;
if s_k=-1, then T_j(c) belongs to B_j exactly for those c with i>=j.

Conversely, suppose b belongs to B_j. Since the first k entries avoid j, define U_j(b)=(u_1,...,u_k) by u_t=b_t if b_t<j and u_t=b_t-1 if b_t>j. Then U_j(b) is a permutation of {1,...,k}, and U_j is the inverse of T_j on the set of all permutations with last entry j. Because U_j is the inverse of the strictly increasing map phi_j, it also preserves order comparisons, so the first k-1 sign conditions hold for U_j(b). If i is the last entry of U_j(b), then b_k=phi_j(i). The last sign condition s_k(b_{k+1}-b_k)>0 means s_k(j-phi_j(i))>0, so it forces i<j when s_k=+1 and i>=j when s_k=-1. Hence U_j(b) lies in the corresponding C_i.

Therefore T_j is a bijection from the disjoint union of the relevant C_i onto B_j: from the union of C_i with 1<=i<=j-1 when s_k=+1, and from the union of C_i with j<=i<=k when s_k=-1. The sets C_i are disjoint because they have different last entries. Taking cardinalities gives
if s_k=+1,
v^(k+1)_j=|B_j|=sum_{i=1}^{j-1}|C_i|=sum_{i=1}^{j-1}v^(k)_i;
if s_k=-1,
v^(k+1)_j=|B_j|=sum_{i=j}^{k}|C_i|=sum_{i=j}^{k}v^(k)_i.
If the index set is empty, the corresponding union is empty and its cardinality is 0, exactly as stated by the empty-sum convention.

Finally, let A be the set of permutations a=(a_1,...,a_n) of {1,...,n} such that s_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)>0 for all 1<=i<=n-1. By definition, |A|=f(s). For each j in {1,...,n}, let A_j be the subset of A with a_n=j. Since a permutation of {1,...,n} has entries exactly 1,...,n, the condition a_n=j is equivalent to saying that a_n is the j-th smallest element. Hence |A_j|=v^(n)_j. The sets A_1,...,A_n are disjoint and their union is A, so
f(s)=|A|=sum_{j=1}^n |A_j|=sum_{j=1}^n v^(n)_j.
This proves the lemma.
solver_summary: Base case is immediate. For the recurrence, fix j and append the value j to a length-k permutation after shifting every old value at least j up by 1; this preserves the first k-1 comparisons, and the final comparison is positive exactly when the old last value i satisfies i<j, and negative exactly when i>=j. This gives a bijection between the relevant stage-k classes and the stage-(k+1) class with last rank j. Summing the stage-n classes over the final rank gives f(s).
vetter_reason: The proof correctly establishes the base case, proves the stated recurrence by an explicit insertion/deletion bijection preserving the first k-1 comparisons and characterizing the last comparison by whether the previous last value lies below or above the inserted value j, and then recovers f(s) by partitioning full permutations according to their final entry. The argument matches the lemma statement and semantic sketch with no substantive drift.
